After a moment, the sibling sets the bag down by the wall, crouches, and points at the boat’s side where the subject has drawn a row of small squares. In English the sibling says, "These look like little windows," then taps one of the stick figures near the edge of the paper and adds, "and this one looks like it’s going to fall in." The subject glances at the spot the sibling indicated, then picks up a darker pencil and begins thickening the line of the pier under the figure while the sibling watches for a few seconds more, straightens up, grabs the school bag and walks on toward the bedroom.

The sibling nods once, says, "Yeah, like that," and continues on toward the kitchen while the subject keeps working on the drawing, now adding a thin line for the upper deck.

episode.observableAction: On a bright mid-morning in the small flat, Caregiver 2 stands by the open kitchen cupboard holding a half-folded paper grocery bag and calls the subject over from the living room, pointing with a free hand at a row of tins and packets on the counter; when the subject comes to the doorway, Caregiver 2 asks them to put all the empty bottles and flattened boxes into the bag so there is space for new shopping, then steps aside to rinse a cup at the sink while glancing back occasionally. The subject moves a chair closer, climbs up to reach the counter, and one by one picks up light plastic bottles and folded cardboard, checks whether anything is left inside, and drops each into the open bag on the floor, sometimes nudging pieces down with a hand so they fit. After the last item is in, the subject pushes the bag upright against the cupboard and says it is finished; Caregiver 2 turns off the tap, comes over, looks into the bag, tucks in a protruding box flap, ties the bag handles loosely together, and tells the subject to leave it by the door for later while the subject drags the chair back under the table and walks toward the living room.

On a dim early evening in the small flat, the subject, their older sibling, and Caregiver 1 sit around the low living room table with an open school science book and a half-finished worksheet between them while street noise filters through the window. Caregiver 1 leans over the book, taps a diagram of the sun and earth with one finger, and tells the subject that it is colder in winter because the earth is farther away from the sun then. The subject, holding a short pencil above the worksheet, pauses and looks from the diagram to the small printed calendar on the facing page that shows months and seasons, then says that summer and winter happen at the same time in places on the top and bottom of the world in a picture they saw at school, so the earth cannot just be closer or farther. The sibling, sitting cross-legged on the floor, glances at the page and adds that their teacher said it was about the tilt. Caregiver 1 frowns slightly, looks back at the diagram, and replies that the important thing is that the sun is not straight above in winter and that is why it is colder, telling the subject to write that it is colder because of the way the earth goes around the sun. After a brief hesitation, the subject bends over the worksheet and slowly writes an answer while Caregiver 1 watches and the sibling shifts to look at the television in the corner.

On a late afternoon in the small flat’s kitchen, the subject stands at the counter with a clear drinking glass half-filled with tap water while their older sibling leans against the doorway holding a school science booklet open to a page with a drawing of a pencil looking bent in water. The sibling taps the picture and says that things always look bent when they go into water because of refraction. The subject frowns slightly, picks up a metal spoon from the draining rack, and slowly lowers the handle into the glass while both of them watch; as the handle passes the water line, it appears offset. The subject lifts the spoon back out, then pushes it in again at a different angle, turning the glass a little with their other hand to see from the side. After looking for a few seconds, the subject sets the spoon down on the counter, takes a short wooden skewer from beside the stove, and repeats the motion, sliding it into the same glass and then pulling it out, glancing between the skewer and the booklet picture while the sibling watches and flips the page back and forth.

On a mid-morning in the municipal school science room, the subject sits at a shared wooden table with a lined notebook open while a science teacher at the front holds up a clear plastic cup of water and tells the class that salt will always dissolve faster in hot water than in cold. After the explanation, the teacher sets two identical cups on a side bench, one just filled from an electric kettle and one from the tap, and pours a spoonful of salt into each, saying they will see the difference later. When the class is told to work quietly, the subject glances toward the bench, then raises a hand and asks if they can try with their own cups. The teacher nods and gestures to a tray of materials. The subject walks up, takes two small plastic cups, a spoon, and a jar of salt, then goes to the sink at the back, runs one cup briefly under the hot tap and the other under the cold, and carries them back to the table. Placing the cups side by side, the subject sprinkles a small, roughly equal pinch of salt into each, starts a wristwatch on the desk, and leans close, stirring each cup once with the spoon and then setting the spoon down. Over the next minute, the subject alternates looking between the two cups, occasionally tilting one slightly to see if any grains remain at the bottom, and glancing at the watch before finally nudging the hot cup forward and pointing at the clearer water when the teacher walks past to check their work.

episode.observableAction: Late on a breezy Saturday morning in the covered market lane, the subject and their older sibling walk slowly past a row of snack stalls with a few coins in the sibling’s hand and the younger child from a neighboring flat trailing beside them, looking back and forth at displays of small pastries, paper cones of roasted nuts, and plastic cups of bright-colored juice. The sibling says they only have enough for one thing to share and tells the younger child to pick, then falls a step behind to watch. The younger child hesitates in front of the pastry case, points at the nuts, then turns toward the juice stand. After a brief pause, the subject nods once and steps away from the wall toward the dusty patch of ground where the others are waiting, while the classmate turns and jogs back, calling out, "Okay, we got one more!"

The subject glances past them at the other children already spreading out into rough positions, then looks back at the classmate and hesitates, shifting their weight from one foot to the other. The classmate tilts their head toward the improvised goal marked by two backpacks and adds, "You can stay near the back if you want, just pass it to me when you get it." After a brief pause, the subject nods once and steps away from the wall toward the dusty patch of ground where the others are waiting, while the classmate turns and jogs back, calling out, "Okay, we got one more!"

In the early evening municipal reading room, the subject and caregiver 2 enter, pause by a temporary exhibition of local paintings, then move to a large dusk ferry-terminal scene near the door; the subject leans in to examine the rough orange and purple brushstrokes on the water, briefly tracing a jagged line in the air near the canvas while caregiver 2 alternates their gaze between the painting and its label, before suggesting they look at the others and leading the subject further down the row.

On a cloudy mid-afternoon after classes, the subject and classmate 1 linger by the low wall near the school gate while most students drift toward the street. Classmate 1 leans their backpack against the wall, glances toward a group of kids laughing by the gate, then turns back and says quietly, "They keep saying Mr. Silva is going to leave next term, but I don’t know if it’s true." The subject shifts their own bag higher on their shoulder and looks over at the same group. Classmate 1 continues, "My cousin says he heard it from his neighbor, but maybe they just made it up. I can’t tell." They pick at a loose bit of mortar on the wall with one finger, then add, "Do you think he’d really go?" and shrug, letting the question hang between them while the noise from the gate carries across the yard.

In a municipal reading room on a drizzly late morning, the subject, their older sibling, and a younger neighborhood child enter the children’s section, where the younger child hesitates between picture books and thin storybooks until the subject crouches beside them, quietly explains the difference between a bright animal picture book and a thinner ferry storybook, and then hands over the ferry book the child points to before returning the animal book and walking with the others toward the borrowing desk.

On a mild Saturday afternoon in the municipal reading room, the subject and their older sibling sit side by side at a long wooden table near the window, each with a different paperback open in front of them. The subject has a school-assigned history book propped against a pencil case, a lined notebook open to a half-filled page, and a ballpoint pen resting across the margin. The sibling leans over from their own seat, taps a paragraph heading in the subject’s book with one finger, and says quietly, "You skipped this part; it’s on the worksheet too." The subject glances at the heading, flips back a page in the notebook, and begins copying a date and short phrase while the sibling straightens up, pulls their own book closer, and resumes reading, occasionally glancing toward the subject’s notes as the room hums with the soft rustle of pages and distant chair scrapes.

On a bright late-morning at the municipal school, the subject lingers at their desk after a science lesson while most classmates file out toward the corridor. The science teacher erases the last chalk diagram from the board, then turns, notices the subject still packing their notebook, and walks over, resting a hand lightly on the edge of the desk. In a conversational tone, the teacher says, "If you like this kind of thing, there’s an extra project group after school on Wednesdays—nothing required, just a few of us doing small experiments and reading a bit more." They slide a half-sheet notice from under their attendance book and place it on the subject’s desk; the paper lists "Optional Science Club" with a time, room number, and a short line about simple experiments. The teacher adds, "You can come by any week and see if you like it; if not, no problem," then straightens up and moves toward the door to speak with another student, leaving the notice in front of the subject as the classroom empties.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: optional after-school science club with extra experiments and reading

episodes.observableAction: On an early Saturday evening in the municipal reading room, the subject and classmate 1 follow a hand-lettered sign to a small exhibition area, slow before a low plinth holding a glass box where bent ferry tickets, rusted screws, and timetable scraps hang in the rough outline of a tilted ferry while faint creaking and water sounds play from a speaker, the subject leaning closer, squinting at the dangling pieces, glancing at the walls and then toward the doorway label reading "Harbor Memory" as classmate 1 tilts their head and quietly asks, "Is this supposed to be the ferry?" before they both stand for a few moments watching the scraps sway.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: "Harbor Memory" mixed-media ferry installation

episodes.observableAction: In the late afternoon, as the regional school bus idles in the gravel lot and students line up to board, the subject stands near the end of the line with a worn backpack hanging from one shoulder, watching a small group of children tossing a foam ball back and forth beside the bus. A slightly taller student with a different route tag clipped to their jacket, person_e2_d2_peer_001, jogs over holding the ball, stops a few steps from the subject, and asks, “You wanna play catch till they let us on?” while lightly tossing the ball once in one hand. The subject shifts the backpack higher, looks toward the open bus door where a driver is talking with another adult, then back at the peer and nods. The peer underhands the ball toward the subject, who reaches out with both hands and catches it against their chest, then throws it back; they continue trading short, careful throws in the dusty space between the bus line and the fence until the driver calls for everyone to get on, at which point the peer gives a quick wave and runs back toward their own bus line while the subject steps into their place in the boarding line, tucking the backpack strap securely onto their shoulder.

Near sunset on a Saturday, the subject walks into the shared hall beside caregiver 1 toward a hand-lettered “Student Art Night” sign, moves to the section labeled with the subject’s grade level, stops in front of a painted board showing a dark blue sky over orange and red hill-like shapes with a single white curved streak, leans in close, tilts their head, traces the air along the white curve without touching, examines the overlapping orange and red brush marks, and steps slightly to the side while caregiver 1 stands behind reading the small name card under the board.

On a cool late afternoon, the subject sits at the kitchen table with an open workbook and dull pencil while caregiver 1 rinses dishes, caregiver 2 leans against the counter with coffee, and the younger sibling rolls a toy car nearby as the subject asks whether the family moved into the current house when they were in first or second grade, prompting caregiver 1 to say it was second grade after winter break and caregiver 2 to say it was before first grade, leading both caregivers to join the subject at the fridge, point to a faded school photo magnet, and continue disagreeing about whether it shows the apartment or the current house while the subject waits with pencil poised over the blank homework line and the sibling watches.

In an eighth-grade science class discussing whether the town should limit lawn watering during dry months, the subject sits quietly at a paired desk between a worksheet and person_e2_d2_peer_001, watching as person_e2_d2_peer_001 argues that restrictions are unfair to families who use small yards for play, the teacher presents a bar chart showing dropping well levels and explains that shared reductions could prevent running out of water and higher costs, person_e2_d2_peer_001 suggests fining only the biggest users instead of a rule for everyone, and the teacher notes enforcement challenges, writes key phrases like “fairness,” “shared resource,” and “target big users?” on the board, and instructs students to write down at least two reasons from either side before continuing the worksheet.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: local water restriction policy debate in science class

episodes.observableAction: During a short break between classes, the subject stands with person_e2_d2_peer_001 and three other students at a courtyard table with club sign-up sheets, declines person_e2_d2_peer_001’s invitation to join the "Rec League Soccer" list, walks over to the quieter "Art & Design Club" clipboard to write their name on a blank line, responds "I’m gonna try this one" when another student asks about soccer, then returns to the edge of the group as the bell rings and they all walk toward the next classroom.

On a cool Saturday evening, the subject walks into the shared hall with caregiver 1 and the younger sibling for a community movie night, passing a folding table where a handwritten sign lists the film title and start time. They find three metal chairs in the middle row facing a portable screen, with other families settling in around them and a faint hum from the projector at the back. The subject sits between caregiver 1 and the sibling, takes a small paper bag of popcorn from caregiver 1, and glances over their shoulder as a volunteer dims the overhead lights. During a brief delay while the projector image flickers and a volunteer adjusts cables, the subject leans toward the sibling, points at the blank screen, and quietly explains that the movie will start once the picture stays on. When the opening scene finally appears and the room quiets, the subject shifts the popcorn bag so the sibling can reach it more easily, then faces forward with the rest of the audience as the film plays.

During an Art & Design Club showcase in the school gym, the subject is called forward by person_e2_d2_teacher_001 to present their poster-sized digital print, presses a remote that fails to change the projected slide, walks to the laptop cart to ask the teacher to try the keyboard, waits as the correct image appears on the screen, then returns beside the easel to briefly describe two details of the projected photo collage before thanking the audience and sitting back with the other club members.

In a winter social studies class, the subject sits in a semicircle as the teacher writes “Community Service Requirement?” on the board, invites opinions, records “time burden,” and later adds the subject’s point about helping groups that need volunteers and a comparison to required gym under pros and cons.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: whether schools should require community service hours for graduation

episodes.observableAction: On a worn couch in the living room after dinner, caregiver_1 sits with the subject tucked against their side and a paperback chapter book open across both their laps. episodes.observableAction: On a windy afternoon at the shared hall during the mobile-library stop, caregiver_1 and the subject step up to a pair of low rolling shelves where paperbacks and slim nonfiction books are arranged with their covers facing out. Caregiver_1 squats beside the subject, runs a hand along a row of animal books, and says the subject can pick one to borrow. The subject scans the covers, pulls out a thin book with a photograph of a tornado on the front, then hesitates and reaches for a different book showing planets against a dark sky. Holding both, the subject looks at caregiver_1, who nods toward the cart and reminds them they can only take one this time. episodes.observableAction: At the cooperative market checkout, caregiver_1 sends the subject to another aisle for a bag of rice; as the subject returns hugging the rice, they slow near caregiver_1 standing behind two adults who quietly argue whether a posted notice means the regional bus schedule or the clinic days are changing, the first waving a folded flyer and insisting the bus is changing, the second pointing toward the entrance schedule and insisting it is the clinic, while the subject glances toward the notice board, then steps beside caregiver_1 and places the rice on the conveyor without speaking.

On an early evening at the cooperative market, caregiver_1 stops with the subject just inside the entrance, hands them a folded ten-dollar bill, and says they need a dozen eggs and a small bag of flour while caregiver_1 goes to the produce section. The subject walks alone down the aisle, pauses to compare two sizes of flour bags, then picks the smaller one and carries it to the refrigerated case, where they open the door, lift a carton of eggs, and check that none are cracked. Holding both items, the subject joins a short checkout line without caregiver_1, sets the flour and eggs on the counter when it is their turn, and answers the cashier’s quiet question about needing a bag by shaking their head and saying, "No, I’m okay." After paying with the bill and taking the change and receipt, the subject tucks the coins into a front pocket, balances the carton and flour in their arms, and walks back toward the produce section, where caregiver_1 is choosing tomatoes.

In a midafternoon social studies class, the teacher presents a proposed phone policy requiring phones to be kept in a locked box all day, asks if anyone disagrees, and the subject raises a hand to say phones should be accessible at lunch for texting parents about rides, repeats this more loudly when prompted, and the teacher notes differing opinions and writes “lunch exception?” on the board while the subject sits back at their desk.

On a Saturday evening in the regional school gym, with folding chairs set up facing a makeshift stage, the subject sits beside other students while teacher_1 introduces a visiting performer and steps back. The performer walks out in work boots and a stained mechanic’s shirt, sets a metal toolbox on a stool, and begins a wordless piece by opening the box and slowly lifting out crumpled grocery receipts, taping them in a line across a clothesline strung between two ladders. Instead of playing music or speaking, the performer keeps adding ordinary objects—an oil rag, a bus ticket, a bent fork—clipping each one to the line until it sags. A few students in the row behind the subject whisper that they thought it was going to be a band. The subject, who came in holding a printed program that just says “Performance: ‘Inventory,’” glances down at the unused microphones at the side of the stage, then back at the silent performer, and stays watching as the performer finally steps away from the crowded line, bows without explanation, and walks off while the gym remains quiet for a moment before scattered clapping starts.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: Silent performance piece 'Inventory' using ordinary objects on a clothesline

episodes.observableAction: On a breezy Friday afternoon, the subject walks down the hallway toward teacher_1’s classroom carrying a spiral notebook and a printed assignment sheet, passing a few students heading for the buses. See office for questions." The subject pauses just inside the room, looks from the empty teacher’s desk to the note, then turns back into the hallway and walks toward the main office, where a line of two other students is already forming at the counter.

The subject shifts the folder to their other hand, peers through the narrow window in the door at the empty room, then turns back down the hallway past a row of locked lockers toward the main entrance, where only a custodian pushing a cart is visible at the far end.

On a warm late afternoon in the dusty backyard, the subject and the younger sibling take turns tossing a scuffed rubber ball at a chalk square drawn low on the exterior wall. After the sibling misses and runs to grab the ball, the subject calls out that misses should mean losing a turn and stepping back to a farther line. The sibling stops, hugs the ball to their chest, and insists that only wild throws that hit the ground first should count as misses. The two stand a few feet apart, pointing at the chalk square and the faint scuff marks on the ground, repeating their versions of the rule and demonstrating throws until they agree that any throw not touching the square lets the other person move one step closer instead of farther. They then mark two new toe lines in the dirt with their heels and resume the game using the adjusted rule.

On a cool Saturday late afternoon, the subject kneels on the living room rug sorting a small pile of school papers into two uneven stacks while a younger sibling sits nearby on a cushion lining up toy cars; Person_e2_d2_caregiver_2 comes in from the kitchen drying their hands on a dish towel, asks which papers need to go back to school, and sits down cross-legged beside the subject as the subject pushes one stack toward the caregiver and says those are for keeping at home, then hands over a crumpled permission slip that the caregiver smooths on their knee, reads, signs on the coffee table, places in a small makeshift envelope labeled with the teacher’s name, and returns for the subject to place in a worn folder with the “school” stack while the sibling drives a toy car in a slow circle around the remaining papers.

On a breezy late afternoon, the subject sits at the small kitchen table with an open spiral notebook, carefully copying a short list of household items from a crumpled note onto a cleaner page while Person_e2_d2_caregiver_1 rinses dishes at the sink and calls out two more things to add. The younger sibling leans against the doorway, swinging one foot and asking what the list is for. After the subject finishes writing, they read the items aloud; the caregiver wipes their hands, comes over to glance at the page, points to one misspelled word and spells it slowly while the subject erases and rewrites it. The caregiver then folds the notebook page, tucks a few bills around it, and slides both across the table to the subject, saying they will take it along on the next trip to the cooperative market, as the sibling steps closer to peer at the folded list before the subject slips it into the front pocket of their worn backpack hanging on the chair.

On a chilly evening at the kitchen table, the subject sits hunched over a half-finished social studies worksheet, slowly copying a few words from an open textbook and pausing with the pencil hovering above the page. Person_e2_d2_caregiver_1 walks in from the hallway carrying a mug, glances down at the worksheet, and asks what it is for. Without waiting for a full answer, the caregiver pulls out the chair beside the subject, sets the mug down, turns the worksheet toward themselves, and begins writing complete sentence answers in the remaining blank lines in their own neat handwriting. The subject rests their forearms on the table and watches while the caregiver fills in the last few questions, then slides the worksheet back, taps the top of the page once, and stands up to carry the mug toward the sink as the subject gathers the finished assignment and tucks it into a worn folder in their backpack on the floor.

On a warm late afternoon in the living room, the subject sits cross-legged on the rug with a small stack of DVDs and a worn portable player open on the coffee table while the younger sibling leans over the arm of the couch watching. The sibling reaches toward two cases at once and asks which one they should watch before dinner. The subject fans out three cases on the table, taps the cover of one with a lot of text and says it is longer and might not fit before they have to stop, then taps another with a darker cover and says it has more talking and fewer funny parts. Finally the subject points to a case with bright colors and says it is shorter and has more of the silly scenes the sibling likes. The sibling studies the three covers, picks up the brightly colored one, and nods. The subject slides the chosen disc into the player, snaps the lid shut, and presses play while the sibling settles onto the couch with a blanket.

On a cool Saturday afternoon at the kitchen table, the subject sits with an open science textbook and a clear glass of tap water, reading a short paragraph that says a small object made of metal will always sink in water. The younger sibling wanders in holding a dull coin and asks what the subject is doing. The subject points to the sentence in the book, takes the coin from the sibling, and says they want to see if it is true. They both lean over the table as the subject slowly lowers the coin flat onto the surface of the water; it slips from their fingers, drops to the bottom of the glass, and comes to rest there. The subject tilts the glass slightly to show the sibling the coin sitting on the bottom, then sets the glass back upright and taps the open page with one finger while the sibling peers down through the water at the coin.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: statement that a small metal object will sink in water

episodes.observableAction: On a breezy Sunday afternoon in the multipurpose hall, folding chairs are set in loose rows facing a collapsible table where a stack of thin paperback booklets with a simple cross on the cover sits beside a plastic pitcher of water. The subject and Person_e2_d2_caregiver_1 take two empty seats near the middle as a middle-aged visitor in a plain shirt stands at the front, hands out the booklets down each row, and asks everyone to turn to a page printed with a short passage from the Gospel of Matthew about loving your enemies and praying for those who persecute you. The subject accepts a booklet passed along the row, flips to the indicated page, and follows the lines with one finger while the visitor reads the passage aloud slowly from their own copy. When the visitor pauses and repeats the sentence about loving enemies, the subject glances once at Person_e2_d2_caregiver_1, then looks back down at the page and keeps their eyes on the printed words until the visitor closes their booklet and begins talking about announcements for the next meeting.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: Gospel of Matthew passage about loving enemies

episodes.observableAction: On a quiet Saturday afternoon at the shared hall during the mobile-library stop, the subject stands in front of a low rolling cart where several paperback novels, a thin poetry collection, and a few non-fiction paperbacks about gardening, astronomy, and local history are propped up with their covers facing out. After scanning the row, the subject picks up the astronomy book, flips through a few pages of star charts, sets it back, then lifts the local history book, briefly reads the back cover, and returns it to the cart. The subject then reaches for the poetry collection, opens it near the middle, reads down one short page, and after a moment closes it and tucks the slim volume under their arm. Without speaking to anyone, the subject walks toward the folding table where the checkout sign is taped, pauses in the short line behind two other patrons, and keeps the poetry book held against their side.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: slim paperback poetry collection from mobile library cart

episodes.observableAction: On a chilly Saturday evening in the shared hall, the subject stands near the back wall with a paper cup of watered-down punch, looking toward a makeshift stage where three local teenagers in plain jeans and hoodies perform a piece advertised on a handwritten flyer as a "dance." Instead of moving in time to the recorded pop song playing softly from a portable speaker, the trio takes turns stepping forward, holding up cardboard signs with short phrases painted in black—"WAITING FOR THE BUS," "NO SERVICE TODAY," "TRY AGAIN LATER"—then slowly tearing each sign into strips and letting the pieces fall to the scuffed floor. Between turns they walk in straight lines, stop, and stand motionless facing different corners of the room while the music continues at the same volume. A few adults seated on folding chairs glance at one another and shift in their seats. The subject, still by the wall, lowers the cup slightly, watches as one performer finally presses the speaker’s stop button so the last sign is torn in silence, and keeps their eyes on the stage while the three teenagers bow once without speaking and step down into the small cluster of people near the front.
